candidates.story: Google Private AI Compute secure server-side memory
candidates.reason: The exact-timestamped architecture change moves private cloud inference from ephemeral processing to persistent per-user state. Google's technical brief and a commissioned Trail of Bits code and threat-model review support a non-duplicate privacy and procurement decision with explicit unresolved limits.

decision.reason: Google's exact-timestamped Private AI Compute update introduces persistent per-user cloud memory and publishes unusually useful architecture and audit evidence. The article explains the operational boundary created by device-held keys, attested enclaves, stateful identity, unresolved deletion rollback and response-derived hashes, without claiming product availability or complete security assurance.

claims.text: Google published the selected page at 16:00:57 UTC on 23 September 2026.
Google says PAIC will add persistent per-user memory whose keys are held on personal devices and whose plaintext is available only inside protected workloads.
claims.sourceLocator: s1 opening and design section; s2 pp. 2 and 9–11.

claims.text: The announcement does not identify the first shipping consumer feature or launch date.
claims.sourceLocator: Complete announcement and future-tense wording at retrieval.

claims.text: The design uses a per-user database in a hardware TEE and mutually attested encrypted channels among memory, orchestration and inference components.
The stateful memory design does not claim network-level non-targetability because a stable per-user identifier is required.
claims.sourceLocator: s2 p. 11 threat model for persistent data.

claims.text: Google commissioned four Trail of Bits consultants for five engineer-weeks of review followed by a fix review and a final report on 21 September.
Trail of Bits found no mechanism for employee plaintext access in the reviewed code.
claims.sourceLocator: s3 pp. 4–5, bounded to reviewed code.

claims.text: The review did not completely assess PAIC, the hardened TPU platform or Oak infrastructure.
The audit reported ten findings and marked eight resolved at fix review.
An unresolved low-severity rollback issue could allow deleted memories to return with persistent privileged storage access and a later user session.
Truncated 96-bit response-derived hashes left the TCB for recitation checking; Trail of Bits rated the issue high and left it unresolved.
Google planned an in-enclave Bloom-filter pre-check, but the final fix review did not mark the hash issue resolved.
The audit was point-in-time, and parts of the wider system remained outside public source and review scope.
Client-side attestation verification and independently witnessed transparency are future work in Google's brief.
A deployment decision should bind the actual product, client and binary to the reviewed design and test its memory lifecycle controls.
claims.sourceLocator: Premises: unknown product availability, audit scope and point-in-time/roadmap boundaries.

notes: Clarified the headline and description so the work reads as a design rather than a shipping product claim.
Added the source-backed exact Google page publication time beside the primary-source link without implying product availability.
Removed an unsupported-sounding value judgement and replaced generic signposts with evidence boundaries or procurement consequences.
Reduced repeated opposition while preserving the separate deletion rollback, response-hash and plaintext-access boundaries.
Preserved the byline, exact disclosure, metadata, links, dates, numbers, audit scope, commissioning relationship, finding counts, future-tense availability and testing limits.
